module_title: Welding and Soldering in Sheet Metal

lessons.title: Safety in Welding and Soldering
lessons.body:
Welding and soldering are high-risk activities. Before you strike an arc or light a torch, put on your personal protective equipment (PPE). For arc welding, you need a welding helmet with a shade 10 or 11 lens for most sheet metal work, leather gloves, a leather apron, and boots. For gas welding, use goggles with a shade 5 lens. Never wear synthetic clothingâit melts and sticks to skin. Cotton coveralls are best.

Ventilation is critical. Welding fumes contain metal oxides and gases that can damage your lungs. Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. If you must work indoors, use a fume extractor or a fan blowing fumes away from your breathing zone. In Africa, many workshops are open-air, which helps, but be aware of wind blowing fumes back at you.

Fire safety: Keep a fire extinguisher (dry powder or CO2) within reach. Remove all flammable materialsâpaint, solvents, rags, paperâfrom a 10-meter radius. Sheet metal can get hot enough to ignite nearby wood or cloth. After welding, stay in the area for at least 30 minutes to watch for smoldering fires.

Gas cylinders require special care. Store oxygen and acetylene cylinders upright and secured with a chain or strap. Keep them at least 6 meters apart or separated by a fire-resistant wall. Never use oil or grease on oxygen fittingsâit can cause an explosion. Open acetylene cylinder valves only 1/4 to 1/2 turn so you can shut them off quickly in an emergency.

Electric shock is a risk with arc welding. Check that your welding machine is grounded. Don't weld in wet conditions. Wear dry gloves and stand on a dry rubber mat if the floor is concrete. If you feel a tingle, stop immediately and have the machine checked.

Finally, protect your eyes from flying chips when chipping slag. Wear safety glasses under your helmet. When you finish, clean up metal scraps and sharp edges. Good housekeeping prevents cuts and trips.

lessons.title: Oxy-Acetylene Welding of Sheet Metal
lessons.body:
Oxy-acetylene welding is ideal for sheet metal because you control the heat precisely. You need an oxygen cylinder, an acetylene cylinder, regulators, hoses (red for acetylene, green or black for oxygen), a welding torch, and a spark lighter. For sheet metal 0.5 mm to 2 mm thick, use a small tip, such as a size 0 or 1. Set the oxygen pressure at 0.2 bar and acetylene at 0.2 bar. Adjust the flame to a neutral flameâa sharp inner cone with no acetylene feather.

Start by cleaning the metal. Remove rust, oil, and paint with a wire brush or grinder. Fit the pieces together with a small gap (about half the thickness of the metal) for butt joints. Tack weld every 25 mm to hold alignment. Use a copper or carbon block behind the joint to absorb heat and prevent warping.

Hold the torch at a 45-degree angle to the joint. Move the flame in a small circular motion to preheat the metal. When a molten pool forms, dip the filler rod (same material as the base metal) into the leading edge of the pool. Add filler only as neededâtoo much causes lumps. Move forward steadily. For thin sheets, use a technique called 'forehand welding' where the torch points in the direction of travel and the filler rod follows.

Control distortion. Sheet metal warps easily. Use clamps or clecos to hold parts. Weld short sections (25-50 mm) and let them cool before continuing. You can also use a heat sink, like a wet rag, next to the weld. After welding, clean the joint with a wire brush and check for cracks or porosity.

In Africa, oxy-acetylene is common because it's versatileâyou can also use it for brazing, cutting, and heating. But acetylene is expensive. If you can't afford it, consider MIG or TIG welding. Always leak-test hoses with soapy water before lighting up. Never use a match or lighterâuse a spark lighter. When finished, close both cylinder valves, bleed the hoses, and back off the regulator screws.

lessons.title: Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (TIG)
lessons.body:
TIG welding (Gas Tungsten Arc Welding) gives you the cleanest, most precise welds on sheet metal. It's perfect for thin stainless steel, aluminum, and even copper. You need a TIG machine with a foot pedal or hand amperage control, a tungsten electrode (2% thoriated for steel, pure tungsten for aluminum), a ceramic cup, and argon gas. For sheet metal 1 mm thick, set the amperage to about 40-60 amps. Use a 1/16-inch tungsten and a #6 or #7 cup. Argon flow should be 10-15 CFH (cubic feet per hour).

Prepare the metal. TIG requires absolutely clean metal. Wipe with acetone or alcohol to remove oil. For aluminum, brush with a stainless steel wire brush dedicated to aluminum only. Fit the joint tightlyâno gap needed for TIG. Tack weld every 20-30 mm. Use a copper backing bar to prevent burn-through on thin sheets.

Hold the torch at a 70-80 degree angle, almost vertical. Strike an arc by touching the tungsten to the work and lifting, or use high-frequency start. Form a molten pool. Dip the filler rod (same alloy as base metal) into the front edge of the pool. Move forward in small steps, adding filler with each dip. For thin sheet, you can often weld autogenously (without filler) for a clean seam. Keep the tungsten sharp and not touching the pool. If it touches, stop, regrind, and restart.

TIG is slow but produces beautiful welds. It's great for visible parts like motorcycle fuel tanks or kitchen equipment. In Africa, TIG is used in workshops that make stainless steel sinks, dairy equipment, and aluminum boats. The main challenge is argon gas supplyâit can be expensive or hard to find in remote areas. If argon is scarce, you might use a MIG welder with CO2, but TIG gives better quality.

Practice on scrap metal. Start with mild steel, then try stainless. Aluminum is trickier because it conducts heat away fastâyou need more amps and a pedal to control heat. Always wear a welding helmet with a shade 10-12 lens. Keep your tungsten clean and your gloves dry.

lessons.title: Gas Metal Arc Welding (MIG)
lessons.body:
MIG welding (Gas Metal Arc Welding) is the easiest welding process to learn and the fastest for sheet metal. It uses a continuously fed wire electrode and a shielding gas. For sheet metal 1-2 mm thick, use a 0.6 mm or 0.8 mm mild steel wire. Set the voltage to 16-18 volts and wire feed speed to 3-4 meters per minute. Use a shielding gas of 75% argon and 25% CO2 (called C25) at 12-15 CFH. For aluminum, use 100% argon and a spool gun or Teflon liner.

Set up your machine. Check the polarity: for solid wire with shielding gas, use DCEP (electrode positive). Install the wire spool, feed it through the liner and gun, and set the tension so the wire doesn't slip but also doesn't crush. Use a contact tip that matches your wire size. For thin sheet, use a 0.6 mm tip with 0.6 mm wire. Clean the metalâremove rust, oil, and paint. Fit the joint with a small gap for butt welds, or overlap for lap welds. Tack weld every 25-50 mm.

Hold the gun at a 10-15 degree angle, pushing the weld (forehand) or pulling (backhand). For thin sheet, push is better for penetration control. Keep a stick-out of 6-10 mm. Move steadily, watching the molten pool. For thin metal, use a series of tack welds (stitch welding) to prevent burn-through. Weld 10-15 mm, then skip 10-15 mm, then weld again. Let each section cool slightly.

MIG is great for production work. In Africa, MIG welders are common in car repair shops, metal furniture makers, and construction. The wire and gas are widely available in cities. If you can't get shielding gas, you can use flux-cored wire (FCAW) which doesn't need gas, but it's messier. Always wear a welding helmet with a shade 10-11 lens. Use pliers to cut the wire between welds. Clean the nozzle regularly with anti-spatter spray.

Practice on scrap. Adjust voltage and wire speed until you get a smooth, crackling sound like frying bacon. If it pops or sputters, adjust. Keep your gloves dry and your work area clean.

lessons.title: Soldering and Brazing Techniques
lessons.body:
Soldering and brazing join metals without melting the base metal. Soldering uses filler metal that melts below 450Â°C, while brazing uses filler that melts above 450Â°C but below the base metal's melting point. For sheet metal, common fillers are 50/50 tin-lead solder (for electrical) or silver solder (for strength). Brazing often uses brass or bronze rods with flux.

Start by cleaning the metal. Remove all oxide with sandpaper or a wire brush. For soldering, apply fluxârosin for electronics, acid flux for sheet metal. Acid flux is corrosive, so clean it off after. For brazing, use borax or commercial brazing flux. Heat the joint with a propane torch or oxy-acetylene torch. For soldering, a small propane torch is enough. For brazing, you need more heatâuse oxy-acetylene with a neutral flame.

Heat the joint, not the filler. Touch the filler to the joint; if it melts, the joint is hot enough. For soldering, apply solder to the joint and let it flow. Don't move the parts until the solder solidifies. For brazing, heat the joint to a dull red, then dip the brazing rod into flux and touch it to the joint. The filler should flow into the gap by capillary action. Use a tight jointâ0.05 to 0.1 mm clearance for soldering, 0.1 to 0.2 mm for brazing.

Soldering is used for electrical connections, radiator repair, and sealing seams. Brazing is stronger and used for bicycle frames, HVAC tubing, and sheet metal assemblies. In Africa, brazing is common in refrigeration repair and car radiators. You can use a charcoal fire with a blowpipe for brazing if you don't have a torchâthis is a traditional method.

After joining, clean off flux with hot water and a wire brush. For soldering, a 60/40 tin-lead solder melts at 190Â°C. For brazing, a typical bronze rod melts at 900Â°C. Always wear safety glasses and gloves. Work in a ventilated areaâflux fumes are harmful. Practice on scrap copper and steel. A good solder joint is shiny and smooth; a good braze joint is golden and filleted.

lessons.title: Spot Welding and Resistance Welding
lessons.body:
Spot welding and resistance welding use electric current and pressure to join sheet metal without filler. Spot welding is the most commonâit's fast and perfect for overlapping thin sheets (0.5-3 mm). You need a spot welder with copper electrodes. The machine passes a high current (1000-10000 amps) through the metal for a short time (0.1-0.5 seconds). Resistance at the joint generates heat, melting and fusing the metal.

Set up your spot welder. For 1 mm mild steel, use a welding current of about 5000 amps and a squeeze time of 0.2 seconds. Adjust the electrode forceâtoo little and you get sparks; too much and you dent the metal. Clean the metal first. Remove paint, rust, and oil. Overlap the sheets by at least 10 mm. Clamp them tightly. Position the electrodes on either side of the joint. Press the foot pedal or trigger. Hold for the set time. Release. You should see a small indentation and a discolored spot. Test the weld by twisting the sheets apartâthe weld should hold.

Spot welding is used in car bodies, appliance manufacturing, and metal furniture. In Africa, many small workshops use foot-operated spot welders for making metal boxes, shelves, and car repairs. If you don't have a spot welder, you can use a carbon arc torch or a MIG welder to make plug welds, but spot welding is faster and cleaner.

Resistance welding also includes seam welding (using rollers) and projection welding. Seam welding makes continuous leak-proof seams for fuel tanks and radiators. Projection welding joins nuts and studs to sheet metal. These processes need specialized machines.

Safety: Spot welders use high currentânever touch the electrodes during operation. Wear dry gloves and stand on a dry floor. Keep the electrodes clean with a file or emery cloth. Replace them when they become pitted. The weld nugget should be 4-5 mm diameter for 1 mm sheet. If the weld is weak, increase current or time. If it burns through, decrease. Practice on scrap. A good spot weld is strong and leaves a slight indentation. Always unplug the machine before changing electrodes.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Welding & Soldering in Sheet Metal â An African Workshop Guide

This practical reference is written for the sheet metal entrepreneur, the artisan fabricator, and the technician running a small workshop in Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, or Johannesburg. It pulls together the six lessons in this module â Safety in Welding and Soldering, Oxy-Acetylene Welding, TIG, MIG, Soldering and Brazing, and Spot & Resistance Welding â into one job-floor decision tool. The goal is not theory for its own sake. It is to help you choose the right process, quote accurately, reduce rework, and win repeat contracts in roofing, HVAC ducting, water tanks, gates, and light structural work.

Across much of sub-Saharan Africa, sheet metal demand is rising with urban housing, cold-chain logistics, and food processing. Yet access to three-phase power, shielding gases, and consumables is uneven. A workshop in an industrial area of Nairobi may run a 300 A MIG set on grid power; a workshop in rural Ghana may depend on a generator and an oxy-acetylene set. The process you choose must match your power, your gas supply, and your client's tolerance for cost and finish.

Why This Matters for African Businesses

Sheet metal work is one of the fastest routes into formal manufacturing for small African enterprises. A two-person workshop with a MIG set, a guillotine, and a bending brake can supply HVAC ducting to a growing hotel sector, fabricate poultry drinkers for agribusiness, or produce stainless steel tables for food processing. Welding and soldering quality directly determines whether you win the next order or absorb the cost of a failed tank, a leaking duct, or a cracked gate hinge.

Three commercial realities shape process choice in most African markets:

  • Power reliability. TIG and MIG require stable voltage. Where the grid fluctuates, an inverter MIG with a generator or a voltage stabiliser is often cheaper than downtime.
  • Gas logistics. Argon and COâ cylinders are available in major cities but expensive inland. Oxy-acetylene remains the most widely available gas process across the continent.
  • Skill supply. TIG welders command higher wages. Training an apprentice on MIG or oxy-acetylene is faster and cheaper for routine sheet metal work.

Process Comparison at a Glance

Table 1 compares the six processes covered in this module across the variables that matter on the workshop floor: thickness range, equipment cost, skill demand, and best-fit applications.

Table 1. Process comparison for sheet metal joining (0.5â6 mm range).
Process Typical thickness Equipment cost (USD) Skill level Best-fit applications
Oxy-Acetylene 0.5â6 mm 300â900 Moderate Repairs, rural workshops, copper/brass, no-power sites
TIG (GTAW) 0.5â6 mm 800â2,500 High Stainless steel food equipment, aluminium tanks, dairy
MIG (GMAW) 1â6 mm 600â2,000 Moderate Ducting, gates, trailers, high-volume production
Soldering 0.2â1.5 mm 50â200 Low Electrical enclosures, gutters, low-temperature joints
Brazing 0.5â3 mm 150â600 Moderate Copper pipework, HVAC, dissimilar metals, radiators
Spot / Resistance 0.5â3 mm 1,000â4,000 LowâModerate Automotive panels, appliance housings, high-volume lap joints

Cost ranges are indicative for small workshops in East and West Africa (2024â2025), based on supplier quotes and Lincoln Electric and ESAB equipment catalogues. Actual prices vary by country, import duty, and currency.

Consumables, Gas, and Cost Drivers

Consumables are where profitability is won or lost. A workshop that tracks filler wire, gas, and flux consumption per job can quote more accurately than a competitor who guesses. Table 2 summarises the key consumables and cost drivers for each process.

Table 2. Consumables, gas, and cost drivers by process.
Process Shielding / flux Filler Main cost driver Africa supply note
Oxy-Acetylene None (flux for cast iron/brazing) Mild steel, copper, brass rods Oxygen & acetylene gas refills Widely available; refills in most towns
TIG Argon (aluminium: AC; steel: DC) ER70S-6, ER4043, ER5356 Argon gas + tungsten electrodes Argon inland is costly; bulk cylinder contracts help
MIG COâ or Ar/COâ mix ER70S-6 wire (0.8â1.2 mm) Wire + gas + contact tips COâ cheap and available; mix less so
Soldering Rosin or acid flux Tin-lead or lead-free solder Solder alloy price (tin-linked) Lead-free solder price volatile
Brazing Borax-based flux Silicon bronze, silver alloys Silver content in filler Silver brazing costly; use Si-bronze where possible
Spot / Resistance None None (parent metal) Electricity + electrode caps Needs stable power; generator sizing critical

Sources: AWS Welding Handbook, 10th ed., Vol. 2; ESAB Consumables Catalogue; Lincoln Electric GMAW Guide; regional supplier pricing (Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, 2024â2025).

â  SAFETY WARNING â READ BEFORE ANY WELDING OR SOLDERING

Welding and soldering produce fumes, intense UV/IR radiation, sparks, and hot metal. In African workshops with limited ventilation, the risks are magnified. Never weld galvanised steel, lead-painted steel, or beryllium alloys without forced-air extraction and a P3 respirator â zinc and lead fume cause metal fume fever and long-term neurological damage. Always wear a welding helmet with correct shade (minimum shade 10 for arc, shade 5 for oxy-acetylene), leather gloves, flame-resistant apron, and closed leather boots. Keep a dry powder or COâ extinguisher within 3 metres. Store gas cylinders upright, chained, with flashback arrestors fitted on both oxygen and fuel lines. Never weld near petrol, paint thinners, or grain dust. Ensure a second person knows where the power isolator and gas shut-off valves are located. If you feel dizzy, stop, move to fresh air, and seek medical help.

Process Notes for the Workshop Floor

Oxy-Acetylene Welding. The most forgiving process for thin sheet in areas with unreliable power. Use a neutral flame for mild steel, a slightly oxidising flame for brass, and a carburising flame for aluminium. Keep the tip size matched to thickness â a #0 or #1 tip for 1 mm sheet. Pre-heat the joint edges, use a small weaving motion, and add filler only when a molten pool forms. Distortion is the main enemy: tack every 50â75 mm and use a copper backing bar where possible.

TIG (GTAW). The premium process for stainless and aluminium. In Africa, TIG is the standard for food-grade stainless steel â dairy tanks, brewing vessels, abattoir tables. Use DCEN for steel and stainless, AC for aluminium. Keep tungsten sharpened to a point for DC, balled for AC. Argon flow 8â12 L/min. Clean the joint with a stainless wire brush dedicated to stainless only â carbon steel contamination causes rust bleed.

MIG (GMAW). The production workhorse for mild steel ducting, gates, and trailers. Use 0.8 mm wire for 1â2 mm sheet, 1.0â1.2 mm for thicker. COâ is cheaper than Ar/COâ mix but gives more spatter; mix gives smoother beads and is worth the extra cost on visible work. Set wire speed and voltage by test coupon, not by guesswork. Keep contact tip and nozzle clean â spatter build-up causes wire feed problems, the most common MIG fault in busy workshops.

Soldering and Brazing. Soldering (below 450 Â°C) suits electrical enclosures, gutters, and low-stress joints. Brazing (above 450 Â°C) suits copper pipework, HVAC, and dissimilar metals. Cleanliness is everything: degrease, then mechanically clean, then flux immediately before heating. For copper pipework, capillary brazing with silicon bronze or silver-bearing filler gives strong, leak-free joints. In food and potable water applications, use lead-free solder and lead-free flux.

Spot and Resistance Welding. Fast, clean, and no filler â ideal for lap joints in appliance housings, automotive panels, and ventilation fittings. The key variables are current, electrode force, and weld time. On thin galvanised sheet, use higher current and shorter time. Electrode caps must be dressed regularly; worn caps cause undersized welds and rejected work. Resistance welding needs a stable power supply â if your workshop runs on a generator, size it at least 2.5Ã the welder's rated kVA to handle inrush current.

Quoting and Quality Control

Quote by the metre of weld, not by the hour, once you know your deposition rate. For MIG on 1.5 mm mild steel, a competent welder deposits roughly 1.5â2.5 kg of wire per 8-hour day on ducting work. Add 15â20 % for setup, tacking, and clean-up. Inspect every joint visually: look for undercut, porosity, incomplete fusion, and spatter. For pressure or water-tight work, dye penetrant or a simple water-immersion test catches leaks before the client does. Document your settings on a job card â repeat jobs become faster and more profitable.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Match process to thickness and power. 0.5â2 mm: oxy-acetylene, soldering, or spot. 1â3 mm: TIG or MIG. 3â6 mm: MIG spray or multi-pass TIG.
  2. Check gas and consumables before starting. Cylinder pressure, wire spool, contact tip, tungsten, flux, and filler rod â running out mid-job wastes time and gas.
  3. Clean the joint. Remove oil, paint, rust, and zinc. Stainless gets a dedicated stainless brush only.
  4. Set up ventilation and PPE first. Forced-air extraction for galvanised or painted steel; helmet, gloves, apron, boots, and respirator as required.
  5. Tack before you weld. Tack every 50â75 mm to control distortion, especially on thin sheet and long seams.
  6. Test your settings on a scrap coupon. Adjust voltage, wire speed, gas flow, and travel speed before touching the customer's job.
  7. Inspect and pressure-test. Visual check for undercut, porosity, and incomplete fusion; water or dye test for leak-tight work.
  8. Record settings and consumables used. A simple job card builds your quoting accuracy and your reputation for repeatable quality.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • American Welding Society (AWS) â Safety and Health Fact Sheets. Free downloadable PDFs on fume control, PPE, and ventilation. aws.org/technical/facts
  • Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) â Welding, Cutting, and Brazing (29 CFR 1910.252). Free official guidance on ventilation, PPE, and fire prevention. osha.gov
  • Lincoln Electric â Welding How-To Guides and Procedure Handbook excerpts. Free technical articles on MIG, TIG, and stick welding settings. lincolnelectric.com
  • ESAB â Knowledge Center and Welding Handbook. Free process guides, consumable selection charts, and troubleshooting tables. esab.com
  • African Development Bank â Industrialise Africa Strategy. Free reports on manufacturing skills and SME development relevant to metal fabrication enterprises. afdb.org

This practical reference is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills programme, Sheet Metal Work course, Module: Welding and Soldering in Sheet Metal. Use it alongside

quiz.q: What is the minimum shade lens recommended for arc welding sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10 or 11 is standard for arc welding sheet metal to protect eyes from UV and infrared radiation.

quiz.q: Why should you never use oil or grease on oxygen cylinder fittings?
options: B) It can cause an explosion
D) It makes the valve sticky
quiz.explanation: Oxygen reacts violently with oil or grease, causing immediate combustion or explosion.

quiz.q: How far should flammable materials be kept from a welding area?
quiz.explanation: A 10-meter radius is recommended to prevent sparks from igniting nearby flammable materials.

quiz.q: What is the correct acetylene cylinder valve opening for quick shutoff?
quiz.explanation: Opening only 1/4 to 1/2 turn allows you to close it quickly in an emergency.

quiz.q: What is the recommended oxygen pressure for oxy-acetylene welding of 1 mm sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: For thin sheet metal, low pressure of about 0.2 bar for both oxygen and acetylene is used.

quiz.q: What type of flame should be used for oxy-acetylene welding of sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: A neutral flame with a sharp inner cone provides the correct heat without adding or removing carbon.

quiz.q: Why is a copper or carbon block used behind a weld joint?
options: B) To absorb heat and prevent warping
C) To make the weld stronger
quiz.explanation: Copper or carbon acts as a heat sink, drawing heat away to reduce distortion.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for TIG welding 1 mm thick sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: For 1 mm sheet metal, 40-60 amps provides enough heat for a controlled weld without burn-through.

quiz.q: Which tungsten electrode type is used for TIG welding aluminum?
quiz.explanation: Pure tungsten is traditionally used for aluminum TIG welding because it maintains a balled tip.

quiz.q: What is the recommended argon flow rate for TIG welding sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 CFH provides adequate shielding without turbulence for most sheet metal TIG welding.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean metal before TIG welding?
options: B) To prevent porosity and contamination
quiz.explanation: Oil, rust, and dirt cause porosity and weak welds in TIG welding.

quiz.q: What should you do if your TIG tungsten touches the molten pool?
quiz.explanation: Touching the pool contaminates the tungsten, requiring regrinding to maintain a stable arc.

quiz.q: What shielding gas mixture is commonly used for MIG welding of mild steel?
quiz.explanation: C25 (75% argon, 25% CO2) provides good arc stability and penetration for mild steel.

quiz.q: What is the recommended wire diameter for MIG welding 1-2 mm sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Thin wire (0.6-0.8 mm) is needed for thin sheet metal to prevent burn-through.

quiz.q: What polarity is used for MIG welding with solid wire and shielding gas?
quiz.explanation: DCEP (electrode positive) provides stable arc and proper penetration for solid wire MIG.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of stitch welding in MIG?
options: B) To prevent burn-through on thin metal
D) To make a stronger weld
quiz.explanation: Stitch welding (welding short segments with gaps) allows heat to dissipate, preventing burn-through.

quiz.q: What is the melting temperature range for soldering?
quiz.explanation: Soldering is defined as joining with filler metals that melt below 450Â°C.

quiz.q: Which flux is recommended for soldering sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Acid flux (zinc chloride) is used for sheet metal because it cleans oxides effectively.

quiz.q: What is the typical joint clearance for brazing?
quiz.explanation: Brazing requires a slightly larger clearance (0.1-0.2 mm) for capillary action of the filler.

quiz.q: What is a common brazing filler metal for sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: Bronze rods are commonly used for brazing sheet metal due to their strength and melting temperature.

quiz.q: How can you braze without a torch in rural Africa?
options: B) Use a charcoal fire with a blowpipe
quiz.explanation: A charcoal fire with a blowpipe can achieve brazing temperatures traditionally.

quiz.q: What is the typical current range for spot welding 1 mm mild steel?
quiz.explanation: Spot welding requires high current (5000-10000 amps) for a short time to fuse the metal.

quiz.q: What is the recommended overlap for spot welding sheet metal?
quiz.explanation: At least 10 mm overlap ensures enough material for a proper weld nugget.

quiz.q: What should you do if a spot weld is weak?
quiz.explanation: Increasing current or weld time adds more heat to form a stronger nugget.

quiz.q: What is seam welding used for?
quiz.explanation: Seam welding uses rollers to create continuous, leak-proof joints for tanks and radiators.

quiz.q: Why must spot welder electrodes be kept clean?
options: B) To ensure good electrical contact
C) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Dirty electrodes increase resistance, causing poor welds and overheating.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a heat sink in welding thin sheet metal?
options: B) To absorb heat and prevent warping
C) To make the weld stronger
quiz.explanation: A heat sink draws heat away from the weld zone, reducing distortion.

quiz.q: What is the correct angle for holding a TIG torch?
quiz.explanation: A near-vertical angle (70-80 degrees) allows good visibility and control of the arc.

quiz.q: What is the recommended filler rod for TIG welding mild steel?
quiz.explanation: ER70S-6 is a common mild steel TIG filler rod.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of MIG welding over TIG?
options: B) Faster and easier to learn
quiz.explanation: MIG is faster and easier to learn because it is semi-automatic and uses a continuously fed wire.
